attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter post, in his own voice.

semantics.note: 'It isn't going to work' is firm language that commits him to an outcome: the scaling bet yields neither AGI nor a product that justifies the costs. It has no deadline. The normalised wording captures both alternatives he named.

contract.note: Reading 'justify the costs' as AI returns that earn back the AI capex is the plain, ordinary reading. The early-resolution rules (an AGI demonstration or payback disclosures; abandonment or impairments) are balanced. The lack of any payback threshold or time frame is flagged correctly.

evidence.note: Dated Nov 2024, before the post. An analyst estimate of about $200B in capex against about $20B of AI revenue describes the starting point, not the outcome of the forecast.

reviews.rationale: This is a firm forecast with no deadline. The packet has no AGI demonstration, no filing showing that AI profits cover capex, and no abandonment or impairment of AI build-outs. The only item is 2024 context. Neither early-resolution rule is met, so the outcome is unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: 'Won't do much more than it can do now' is a firm forecast measured against December 2024 capability. 'Over-leveraged' is a vague characterisation; the contract rightly leaves it unscored.

contract.note: The plain reading (no major new capability beyond December 2024 frontier models) is ordinary and fair. An officially graded IMO gold is a reasonable test of 'much more': it is a recognised hard task, not a gameable benchmark. 'Much more' has no threshold, so the interpretation drives the result.

evidence.note: Dated July 2025, after the baseline. A secondary account quotes DeepMind saying IMO coordinators officially graded its model at gold level. The certification claim comes via the lab, but the blog's author independently discusses the result and the contest context.
Sets the baseline: in 2024 an IMO silver needed formal systems, manual translation and days of compute. In 2025 a single natural-language model scored gold within contest time.
METR, March 2025, independent. It shows a roughly 7-month doubling trend in task length, but the excerpt does not isolate a clear post-December-2024 jump, so it is only supporting context.

reviews.rationale: The early-resolution rule is met. In July 2025 a generative AI model received an officially graded IMO gold, a result no generative model had achieved by December 2024 (2024 needed specialised formal systems for a silver). That is a clear capability gain beyond the baseline, so the forecast is contradicted. The 'over-leveraged' part is not scored.

attribution.note: His own words. The 200M weekly-user figure is marked 'allegedly' and is not his claim; the loss and adoption assertions are his.

semantics.note: This describes the state of affairs at the time of the post. The normalised wording keeps both the loss assertion and the adoption assertion and correctly leaves out the 200M figure.

contract.note: Plain readings are used: the loss is read as costs exceeding revenue, not a per-prompt figure, and 'actual generative AI software' as paid business products, which matches his Copilot example. That is fair. 'Widespread' has no threshold, and the surveys measure different populations, so interpretation decides the result.

evidence.note: Census BTOS: about 4-5% of US firms used any AI, Sep 2023 to Feb 2024. This supports low adoption, though the measure is broader than generative AI.
Census: the AI use rate among the largest firms stayed under 8% through August 2024. Published on the post date. Supports limited adoption.
A Microsoft company disclosure (October 2024) that nearly 70% of the Fortune 500 use M365 Copilot. It cuts against his claim for large firms, but it is a self-report with no seat depth.
McKinsey's 2024 survey: 65% of respondents' organisations regularly use generative AI. This points toward broad use among respondents, but it is a survey sample, not all firms.

The Information's 2024 estimates: about $4B of inference spending against $3.5-4.5B of total revenue, with ChatGPT around $2B. This is consistent with a loss but does not separate ChatGPT's serving cost.

reviews.rationale: The adoption evidence conflicts. Census shows single-digit AI use across firms, while Microsoft's disclosure and McKinsey's survey show majority use among large firms or survey respondents, so both the contract's support and contradiction conditions are partly met. The ChatGPT loss part cannot be confirmed because no 2024 source separates ChatGPT's serving cost from its revenue. The packet does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Two parts: big tech, including Amazon at up to $75B in 2024, spending heavily on AI data centres, and business integration of generative AI not appearing to happen at scale. 'Does not appear' describes the observed state; it is not probabilistic hedging.

contract.note: The two-part split and the 2024 period are fair. Reading 'at scale' as broad deployment beyond pilots at a small share of firms is ordinary. The populations measured differ, so interpretation decides the adoption part.

evidence.note: Amazon guided to about $75B of 2024 capex, driven largely by generative AI demand. This matches his 'as much as $75 billion'. It is guidance, not final actuals.
Census: about 5% of US firms used any AI in early 2024. This supports 'not at scale' across the economy.
Microsoft company disclosure: nearly 70% of the Fortune 500 use Copilot. It cuts against his claim for large enterprises, but it is self-reported and gives no depth of deployment.
McKinsey's 2024 survey: 65% of respondents' organisations regularly use generative AI. This points toward broad use among the surveyed organisations.

reviews.rationale: The spending part is supported: Amazon guided to about $75B for 2024, mostly for AI. The central adoption part is not settled. Census shows low use across all firms, while Microsoft's disclosure and McKinsey's survey show majority use among large firms or survey respondents, and no source measures production integration at scale directly. With the core conjunct unsettled, the claim as a whole is unresolved.
